title: Who Gets to Decide What Goes on a Map
hook: Renaming a lake is not a matter of announcing it. In the U.S. a name normally climbs from town to county to state to a federal board — and stops entirely at the border.
key_points: The U.S. Board on Geographic Names, housed in the U.S. Geological Survey, standardizes place names for the federal government.
The usual path is bottom-up: a community proposes, local and state bodies sign off, then the federal board makes the name official nationwide.
Minneapolis's Lake Calhoun became Bde Maka Ska in 2018 by exactly that route — park board, county, state, then the federal board.
The executive branch can shortcut it: the law lets the Interior secretary act when the board delays unreasonably, as with Denali in 2015.
Authority stops at the water's edge — a shared or international feature can be renamed only on U.S. maps; other countries keep their own names.
Digital maps now show different names to different users: Google displays the U.S. official name to U.S. users and Mexico's to Mexican users.
content_html: Renaming a place sounds like a decision someone simply makes. In practice the United States runs a slow, layered procedure. The U.S. Board on Geographic Names, part of the U.S. Geological Survey, standardizes names for federal use, and its members are appointed by the Interior secretary with input from state, local and tribal authorities. A change usually starts at the bottom: a community proposes it, local governments endorse it, the state weighs in, and only then does the federal board make it official. Minneapolis took Lake Calhoun to Bde Maka Ska that way in 2018.
extra_html:
Writing in The Conversation, geographer Innisfree McKinnon notes the process has an express lane. The law permits the Interior secretary to act when the board has delayed unreasonably — how Denali became official in 2015, four decades after Alaska first asked. Recent executive orders renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Mount McKinley used the same top-down channel, and the 2026 order on Lake Ontario followed it.

The harder limit is geographic, not procedural. A feature shared with another country, or lying beyond U.S. territorial waters, can be renamed only for U.S. purposes; Mexico still prints "Gulf of Mexico," and Canada is not obliged to accept "Lake America." What is new is that the disagreement is now rendered per-user: mapping platforms display each nation's official name to that nation's viewers, so two people can look at the same app and see two different countries' politics.

related.title: Maps as Political Power
related.hook: A map looks like neutral fact, but someone chose what to show, what to leave out, and where to draw the line — and those choices shape voting, travel, and spending.

related.title: What Federalism Is
related.hook: Some countries split authority between a national government and regional ones, each with powers the other can't simply override.

related.title: Sovereignty Among Nations
related.hook: Inside its borders a state is supreme — but in the world of states there's no higher ruler. That gap, called anarchy, shapes everything about international politics.

related.title: What an Executive Order Can and Cannot Change
related.hook: A presidential order can tell the executive branch what to aim for. It can't skip the process an agency must follow — which is why headlines and reality often diverge.

flashcards.prompt: What is the normal route for officially renaming a place in the United States?
flashcards.back_html: Bottom-up: a local proposal gathers community and local-government support, moves through state authorities, then reaches the U.S. Board on Geographic Names, which makes it official for federal use.

flashcards.prompt: A U.S. president renames a body of water shared with another country. What actually changes?

choices.text: Only U.S. official usage — the other country keeps its own name
The name changes worldwide once the federal board records it
Nothing, because presidents have no role in place naming at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Naming authority is territorial. The U.S. can standardize a name for its own maps and agencies; a neighboring state is under no obligation to follow.

flashcards.prompt: Why can the same lake appear under two different names on the same mapping app?
flashcards.back_html: Major platforms display names by the viewer's country, following each government's official designation — so users in different countries see different labels for the same feature.
